facts.label: Town mayor
facts.description: Edric Vale serves as the town's mayor.

facts.label: Moonflowers
facts.description: Edric has a particular fondness for Moonflowers.

facts.label: River fishing
facts.description: Edric values quiet mornings spent fishing by the river.

nodes.text: A new face warrants a proper welcome—and a little context. What brings you to our town?

choices.text: I hope to help wherever the town needs me.
I'm still finding my way around.

nodes.text: Civic spirit is always welcome. I shall remember that offer.
Sensibly cautious. Take time to learn which paths—and people—deserve your trust.
I hear you have begun exploring Moonwood. Stay to the marked paths; appearances there can mislead.
Moonwood has drawn you back more than once. Curiosity is useful when tempered by judgment.
You found **Moonflowers**. Their color survives even the gloomiest council chamber; I have always admired that.

choices.text: Then please accept one.

nodes.text: Good to see you again. How is village life treating you?

choices.text: I brought you a Moonflower.

nodes.text: A thoughtful choice. Thank you—I shall see it placed where the morning light catches it.
You have earned the standing of Acquaintance. In public life, dependable gestures carry considerable weight.

facts.label: Town archivist
facts.description: Helena Vale keeps Alderwake's town archives and helps residents trace public records.

facts.label: Careful records
facts.description: Helena cross-checks every archive entry before treating it as settled history.

facts.label: Pressed Moonflowers
facts.description: Helena presses Moonflowers to preserve seasonal color beside dated archive notes.

nodes.text: I'm Helena Vale. You will usually find me among the **town archives**, making certain yesterday remains useful tomorrow.

choices.text: I would rather check a story than repeat it carelessly.
I mostly hope to learn my neighbors' names.

nodes.text: Good. A careful question leaves less damage than a confident mistake.
A sound beginning. Names are the first index any town keeps.
Those would make lovely **pressed Moonflowers**. Their color marks a season more honestly than ink alone.

choices.text: Then please keep one for the archive.

nodes.text: Welcome back. Have you found anything in Alderwake that deserves a closer look?

choices.text: I brought a Moonflower for your seasonal notes.

nodes.text: Thank you. I will press it beside today's date and credit the collector.
Mind the open folios, please. I **cross-check every entry** before returning a page to its box.

choices.text: I will let you continue.
The light is fading; perhaps stop here for today.

nodes.text: One moment. This index says the volume is here, while the shelf insists otherwise.

choices.text: Keep tracing it; I can wait.
I noticed a ledger reference that does not match the index.
Leave the mismatch marked and rest for today.

facts.highlightTerm: line, hooks, rope and lamp oil

facts.label: Decorative knots

choices.text: I would rather choose sound gear than replace it halfway.
I am passing through and learning my way around.

nodes.text: A sensible start. A little attention now saves a wet walk later.
Then take your time. River work makes more sense when you have seen the river.
Welcome back. What can I help you understand?

choices.text: What ordinary supplies do you keep?
How do you choose a fitting?
What do you make when work is done?
I brought a Moonflower for your work table.

nodes.text: We keep **line, hooks, rope and lamp oil** for everyday jobs. Tell me what you need before choosing a fitting.
A fitting has to suit the load and the hands using it. Guesswork can look very neat until it gets wet.
Small **decorative knots**, with no boat depending on them. A Moonflower beside the tea makes the table a pleasant place to sit.
Thank you. That will brighten the table while I finish this knot.

Take your time on the public quay. A busy dock rewards a patient pair of eyes.
Good to see you. What would you like to know?

facts.label: General goods
facts.description: Tess Reed runs Alderwake's general store, carrying staples, cloth, household goods and packed trail food.

facts.label: Everyday supplies
facts.description: Tess starts with practical everyday needs and welcomes supply questions without requiring favors.

facts.label: Pressed flowers
facts.description: Tess keeps pressed flowers in a small book; she welcomes a Moonflower for its next page.

nodes.text: Tess Reed. I keep the **general goods** here. Tell me what you need, and leave room for the next person at the door.

choices.text: I will start with what people need.
I am looking around town.

nodes.text: A good place to start. A useful parcel matters more than a grand gesture.
Take your time. You can ask a practical question before we have become old friends.
Hello again. What is on your mind?

choices.text: What supplies do people ask for?
How would I arrange useful delivery work?
Is keeping the store tiring?
What do you do away from the shelves?
I brought a Moonflower for your book.

nodes.text: We start with **everyday supplies**: staples, cloth and packed trail food. Ask for what you need; favors are never an entry fee.
Useful help starts with a clear list: what needs carrying, where, and for whom. I check those details before making an arrangement.
Some days. A cup of tea between columns helps. Listening is easier when I remember to sit down.
I keep **pressed flowers** in a little book. Each page asks me to slow down. A Moonflower would make a lovely next page.
Thank you. I will make room for it in the book.

facts.description: Ivo Oran is Alderwake's river-run captain and fishmonger. He handles passenger-berth business and local fish supplies.

facts.label: Local seamanship
facts.description: Ivo knows ordinary fishing and local seamanship, checking weather, lines and a clear shore before work.

facts.label: Knotwork
facts.description: Ivo practices knotwork and keeps river notes in a small book; he likes a pressed Moonflower between its pages.

nodes.text: Ivo Oran, **river-run captain** and fishmonger. Keep the shore lane clear and tell me what you need.

choices.text: I will keep clear of the working lines.
I am getting to know the docks.

nodes.text: Good. Room to work is useful help.
Ask away. You need not bring a favor to ask a question.
Back at the river. What is on your mind?

choices.text: What keeps local fishing work going?
How do you plan a job by the water?
Do you ever put the work aside?
What do you do between trips?
I brought a Moonflower for your river book.

nodes.text: Ordinary fishing and **local seamanship**: watch the weather, check the lines, keep a clear shore. A small useful catch still feeds someone.
First agree what needs doing and who is helping. Then check the lines, gear and footing together. A confident promise is no substitute for a sound plan.
Eventually. Tea on dry ground is a fine invention. Tomorrow is easier to think about after a sit-down.
I practice **knotwork** and keep river notes in a little book. A pressed Moonflower makes a good bookmark; it reminds me to slow down.
Thank you. There is a clean page waiting for it.

facts.label: Boatwright
facts.description: Celia Oran is Alderwake's boatwright. She checks old hulls carefully and repairs what can safely be kept.

facts.label: Basic repairs
facts.description: Celia can inspect seams, mend fittings and make basic repairs. These ordinary skills are distinct from her advanced hull-shaping technique.

facts.label: Woodcarving
facts.description: Celia enjoys woodcarving, making small river birds from spare wood. She likes keeping a Moonflower beside the finished carvings.

nodes.text: Celia Oran, **boatwright**. I would rather mend a sound old hull than throw it away. Mind the fitting tray, and ask what you need.

choices.text: I will leave room for your work.
I am looking around town.

nodes.text: Thank you. A clear work space makes careful hands more useful.
Then ask away. Looking costs nothing.
What would you like to know?

choices.text: What ordinary repairs can you help with?
Tell me about your fair boat.
Do you ever put the tools down?
What do you make for yourself?
I brought a Moonflower for your carvings.

nodes.text: I can help with **basic repairs**: inspect a seam, mend a fitting, replace a worn line. Those are useful skills of their own. Advanced hull shaping is a different kind of judgment.

My small shallow-water demonstration boat is for a short fair ride back to the same bank. It is separate from the passenger ship, and from an heirloom skiff. A demonstration is no replacement for an onward passage.
Eventually. Tea first, then I can decide whether that seam truly needs another look.
I enjoy **woodcarving**: little river birds from spare wood. A Moonflower beside them makes the work bench feel less like a list of jobs.
Thank you. I will give it a place beside the birds.

facts.label: Innkeeper
facts.description: Della Pike is the innkeeper at Lantern Rest, welcoming visitors and neighbors to its meal room.

facts.label: Quiet company
facts.description: Della offers quiet company without asking people to explain private matters. Guests may ask for space or conversation.

facts.label: Quilting
facts.description: Della enjoys quilting with useful scraps of cloth. She likes a Moonflower beside her sewing basket.

nodes.text: Della Pike, **innkeeper** at Lantern Rest. I am meeting visitors here at the public entrance. Questions and quiet company are welcome; the inn interior is not open in this prototype.

choices.text: Thank you. I will leave space for the other guests.
I am getting to know the town.

nodes.text: That is thoughtful. You need not earn a welcome, though.
Then take your time. Questions are welcome here.
What would you like to know?

choices.text: How do you look after your guests?
May people keep their troubles private?
Which part of the inn is the guest room?
Do you ever sit down yourself?
What do you enjoy when the work is done?
I brought a Moonflower for your sewing basket.

nodes.text: A warm meal room, a clear way through the door, and someone who listens. Guests and neighbors can both ask me a question.
I offer **quiet company**, too. No one owes a story in return for care. If you want space, say so; if you want to talk, I can listen.
The guest room is on the right, off the main passage. The meal room is here on the left. Keep the passage clear so everyone can come and go.
I do, once the room settles. A cup of tea stays warmer when I remember to drink it.
I enjoy **quilting**, giving scraps of cloth a useful second life. A Moonflower beside my sewing basket makes a quiet hour feel special.
Thank you. I will put it beside the basket.
